untyped_cells.text: Medulloblastomas (MBs), molecularly defined Medulloblastomas, WNT‐activated b Medulloblastomas, SHH‐activated and TP53 ‐wildtype b Medulloblastomas, SHH‐activated and TP53 ‐mutant b Medulloblastomas, non‐WNT/non‐SHH (Groups 3 and 4)

Other CNS embryonal tumors c Atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumor (AT/RT) Cribriform neuroepithelial tumor (CRINET) d Embryonal tumor with multilayered rosettes (ETMR) CNS neuroblastoma, FOXR2‐activated CNS tumor with BCOR internal tandem duplication (BCOR ITD) e CNS embryonal tumor, NEC/NOS
RL I: Histology only + special stains
RL II: + Basic diagnostic IHC markers (GFAP, S‐100, Ki‐67, EMA, CD34)
Level 1: Microscope, H&E staining, CSF cytology
RL III: + Surrogate IHC molecular markers (IDH1p.R132H, ATRX, H3p.K27M, H3p.K27me3, L1CAM…)
Level 2: Limited IHC panel (disease‐specific), Cytospin for CSF samples
RL IV: + Basic molecular tests (FISH, Sanger, PCR)
Level 3: Complete IHC panel, molecular pathology for most diseases
RL V: + Advanced molecular tests (NGS, DNA methylation profiling)
Level 4: Research diagnostics, whole genome sequencing, molecular pathology for all diseases
20% of all MBs (in children <3 years 40%–50%; in adults 20%–40%)
Wide age range, predominantly in children (60%–70%)
Bimodal: infant and young children (<3 years); can occur in adults as well
All ages, but predominantly in children
Cerebellar hemispheres (esp. in adults) and midline (more in infants)
Cerebellar midline with variable involvement of hemispheres
More common than in other subtypes
Densely packed poorly differentiated small round blue cells; high N:C ratio; hyperchromatic nuclei; frequent mitoses; apoptotic bodies; Homer Wright rosettes (~40%)

Nodular architecture with desmoplasia; Reticulin‐free “pale” nodules of neurocytic differentiation with internodular poorly differentiated hyperchromatic cells in reticulin‐rich stroma; no Homer Wright rosettes

Expanded nodular architecture with often large, confluent, reticulin‐free nodules with neurocytic streaming in a fibrillary neuropil‐like background; Limited internodular component of poorly differentiated cells (much less extensive than in D/N MBs); low mitotic activity

Large pleomorphic cells, with prominent nucleoli, and nuclei ×3 size of RBC, with high mitotic activity and abundant apoptosis; tumor cell wrapping; nuclear molding; nuclear pseudoinclusions; no rosettes/desmoplasia
Synaptophysin (+), NeuN (+), MAP2 (+), NSE (+); OTX2 (+) with the exception of classic MB SHH‐activated
Synaptophysin (+) and NeuN (+) in nodules; MIB‐1 relatively high in internodular areas, while lower in nodules; OTX2 (−)
Synaptophysin and NeuN (+) in nodules; OTX2 (−)
Predominant molecular group (RL III and IV)
All molecular groups—More commonly WNT‐activated and non‐WNT/non‐SHH (Groups 3 and 4)
Infants and children <3 years almost always SHH‐activated, TP53 ‐wildtype Children (>3 years), teenagers and adults—can be SHH‐activated, TP53‐ mutant or TP53 ‐wildtype
Excellent in infants and young children <3 years
Excellent, even in metastatic cases (PFS and OS reaching 100% in some studies)
Worst among histologic types; 5‐year PFS 30%–40% (high‐risk category).
Non‐infant children (most often 7–14 years) and adults (15% of MBs in the latter group)
Bimodal age distribution; Infants and children (<3 years) and adults
More in infants (40%–45%) and in children; Rare in adults
All age groups—peak incidence 5–15 years; Lower incidence in infants and adults
Midline with extension to cerebellar peduncle, cerebellopontine angle and lateral recess of 4th ventricle; close to/abutting the brainstem
Lateral (cerebellar hemisphere); abutting on the tentorium esp. in adults MBEN and D/N in infants show midline location
Midline and 4th ventricle; caudally located displacing the dorsal brainstem
Variable, heterogeneous; MBEN hypointense with grape‐like nodular appearance
No edema, metastasis rare; lobulated margins; dorsal brainstem infiltration
Tumor margins infiltrative; significant peritumoral edema; metastases rare
Early leptomeningeal spread; laminar sugar‐coating metastasis pattern in the leptomeninges
Macrocysts; early non‐enhancing nodular ependymal metastases; enhancing leptomeningeal metastases may also be seen
Histological type(s), molecular alterations and prognosis
Predominant Molecular alterations (RL III and IV)
PTCH1 deletion; PTCH1 / SMO / SUFU mutation
Favourable prognosis, esp. D/N and MBEN in infants (5 years OS ~75% to 80%)
Poor outcome; worst in those with MYC amplification (5 year OS ~50%). Metastasis ~45%
Positive (nuclear), (better assessed on oil immersion lens)
Negative in tumor cell nuclei (but may be cytoplasmic/membranous positive)
Negative in tumor cell nuclei (but may be cytoplasmic/membranous positive)
WT pattern versus Mutant pattern (in the latter: diffuse strong staining of tumor cell nuclei or complete absence of staining of these nuclei)
For diagnosis of D/N and MBEN
Diffuse immunopositivity in most MBs; dot‐like/speckled in LC/A
Other neuronal markers (NSE, MAP‐2, Nestin and NeuN)
Diffuse or focal positive in most MBs
Positive (nuclear) in some classic MBs (except classic MB, SHH‐activated) and negative in D/N MBs and MBEN
Negative in tumor cells (reactive astrocytes positive in the background)
Positive in MB, but also in AT/RT and CNS tumor with BCOR ITD
Negative in MB Helps to rule out CNS NB FOXR2 ‐activated
Negative in MB Helps to rule out AT/RT (positive)
Negative in MB Helps to rule out CNS NB FOXR2 ‐activated
Positive in MBs and CNS tumor with BCOR ITD
Helps to differentiate from ETMR which is positive for CD99. Also positive in Ewing Sarcoma
To rule out AT/RT if histology is of classic or LC/A MB and especially in children less than 3 years of age; Retained nuclear staining in MB and loss in the vast majority of AT/RTs
If there is high suspicion of AT/RT and INI‐1 is negative; Retained nuclear staining in MB and loss of staining in AT/RTs with preserved SMARCB1 nuclear staining
Negative in MB; Helps to rule out ETMR which shows strong and diffuse immunopositivity for LIN28
Negative in MB; Helps to rule out CNS tumor with BCOR ITD which shows widespread strong nuclear expression of BCOR
β‐catenin, GAB‐1, YAP‐1, Filamin A, OTX‐2, p75‐NGFR, LEF1
For determination of Molecular grouping (surrogate markers)—panel of 3–4 markers can be used as per choice of institution (see text and Table 4 for details)

Mandatory for D/N and LC/A histology and SHH‐activated MBs. Optional in WNT MBs. Strong diffuse or complete absence of nuclear staining in SHH‐activated TP53 ‐mutant (see Resource Level V of this table as well as text of paper for details).
For non‐WNT/non‐SHH MB irrespective of histological type—suggests group 3 MB associated with poor prognosis (no surrogate IHC available).
For non‐WNT/non‐SHH and SHH‐activated TP53 ‐mutant MBs—associated with poor prognosis (no surrogate IHC marker available)
For WNT‐activated MB if IHC for β‐catenin and/or other markers in IHC panel are equivocal (no surrogate IHC marker available)
For SHH‐activated MB especially with LC/A histology and/or if IHC staining for p53 is negative (null staining)/focal/equivocal. in suspected cases of germline mutation of TP53 (Li‐Fraumeni syndrome)
Molecular group (esp. Groups 3 and 4) and subgroup
For molecular classification of MBs, esp. cases discordant on IHC/FISH/Sanger sequencing/NGS
60% infratentorial (cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellopontine angle and brainstem); 40% supratentorial; rarely suprasellar, pineal, spinal
70% supratentorial (mainly cerebral hemispheres) 30% infratentorial (cerebellum and brainstem)
Supratentorial (cerebral hemisphere); infratentorial (cerebellar hemisphere) Rarely in brainstem, cerebellopontine angle, spinal cord
Cysts, necrosis, and hemorrhage typical; leptomeningeal spread in ~20%–30%
Predominantly solid; cysts and calcification occasional
Solid tumor; central cystic component common
Well circumscribed large; solid ± cystic component; no or minimal perilesional edema
Rhabdoid cells may be present; Variable population of primitive cells with divergent differentiation (mesenchymal, epithelial, primitive embryonal); brisk mitotic activity, necrosis, hemorrhage
Broad histologic spectrum; true ependymoblastic rosettes—multilayered rosettes with mitoses Three variants—ETANTR, Ependymoblastoma and Medulloepithelioma
Primitive neuroepithelial cells with high‐grade features in a fibrillary glioma‐like background; ependymoma‐like perivascular rosettes present
Sheets of poorly differentiated embryonal cells; neuropil like stroma; Homer Wright rosettes and ganglion cells may be seen
Highly cellular with small cells arranged in cribriform strands and ribbons; rhabdoid cells absent.
Polyimmunophenotypic with variable positivity to Vimentin, EMA, SMA, CK, GFAP and synaptophysin
Embryonal component: Vimentin (+), strong; Nestin (+); GFAP, EMA, CK, CD99 (±), focal Neuropil‐like matrix: Synaptophysin (+), strong; NeuN (+); NFP (+)
Olig2 (+, strong); Synaptophysin (+); MAP2 (+); GFAP (−); Vimentin (−); SOX10 (+); TTF1 (+)
Vimentin (+), synaptophysin (+); MAP2 (+); EMA (±), highlights cell surface; GFAP variable; Tyrosinase (+)
Tumor cell nuclei: INI1 loss OR INI1 retained but BRG1 loss ASCL1 (+) and Tyrosinase (+) in AT/RT—SHH and AT/RT—TYR subtypes respectively
Mutation or loss of SMARCB1 locus at 22q11.2 (95%); SMARCA4 alteration (<5%)
Amplification or fusion of microRNA cluster on chromosome 19q13.42 (C19MC ~ 90–95% of cases) DICER1 mutation in ~5% cases
Heterozygous internal tandem duplication (ITD) in exon 15 of BCOR gene
FOXR2 activation by complex inter chromosomal and intra‐chromosomal rearrangements; Gain of 1q
Biallelic SMARCB1 inactivation; (often large deletion of 22q associated with mutation in remaining allele).
